## Invasive populations {#sec-invasions}

Mainly from deer parks and private collections

### Invasive populations in Europe

The introduction of the species to Europe has primarily occurred through deliberate releases and escapes from captivity, originally for ornamental purposes, game ranching, and private collections.

The species was first introduced to the **UK** in the early 20th century, with individuals released into the wild for aesthetic and sporting (i.e., hunting) reasons.
Additional introductions and escapes from private estates and zoological collections further contributed to its spread, as the species is relatively easy to keep and breeds readily in captivity.
In the decades following its introduction, the Chinese muntjac became firmly established in the UK countryside, particularly across central and southern England, where it has since undergone substantial population growth and range expansion (ref section biology).

Beyond the UK, established populations of the Chinese muntjac have also been reported from several regions in continental Europe, **mainly France, Ireland, and Belgium**.

In France, recent observations confirm a small, but likely expanding population in the Centre-Val de Loire region, where animals are thought to have originated from escapes or releases near zoological or private facilities.
In Ireland, the species was introduced in 2009 and is considered established, spreading from Northern Ireland to other parts of the island.
In Belgium, the species has been recorded since at least the early 2000s, with the core of the current free-ranging population located on the eastern edge of the Antwerp agglomeration (see following section).

Additional isolated observations elsewhere in Europe, **including the Netherlands, Denmark and Germany**, have so far not led to confirmed self-sustaining populations.

### Invasive population in Flanders

#### Invasion history

The invasion history in Flanders [cf. @casaer_best_2015; @dhondt_monitoring_2023] begins in 2005, with a roadkill victim in the province of Limburg.
2009 marks the year with the first confirmed observation of a living specimen in the wild, in Schoten in the province of Antwerp. 
In addition, hunters reported sightings in the Zoerselbos (also Antwerp).
While there were only a few sightings between 2010 and 2012, 
numbers started to rise afterwards, and the distribution of occurrences also expanded.
This expansion can be closely linked to animals having escaped or been released from illegal private collections.
By 2015, the species had been observed in all Flemish provinces.
In 2020, the number of number of 1 x 1 km grid cells with sightings reached a maximum (66 grid cells) and has declined since then (to be verified using GBIF data > 2022).

By 2025, the Flemish Chinese muntjac population has established itself in the **province of Antwerp**, including the municipalities of Schoten, Brasschaat, and Wuustwezel.
The invasion stadium of the species can be considered as 'established to limited extent' [@dhondt_een_2022].
 

#### Current distribution

Within the current distribution area in the Antwerp province, 
the species is particularly established in the fragmented landscape of urban-adjacent forest patches, parks, and green corridors
east of the city of Antwerp [@dhondt_monitoring_2023]. 
This prominently features the domain Park Vordenstein, a largely state-owned, public recreational domain.
On that 137 hectares sized domain, specimens of Chinese muntjac have been reported from 2012 onwards, 
with more recent observations stemming from camera trap-based monitoring conducted by ANB and INBO between 2020 and 2024 [@dhondt_monitoring_2023; @neeckx_occurrence_2024] (ref sec monitoring).
Although the overall distribution remains relatively localized, the population shows signs of spatial expansion, with detections in nearby municipalities suggesting ongoing dispersal.



```{r fig-gbif-occ}
#| include: true
#| message: false
#| results: 'hide'
#| fig-cap: "Occurrences of the Chinese muntjac in and around Flanders according to GBIF"
#| out-width: 100%

gis_data_path <- "../../data/gis"
gbif_data_file <- "../../data/gbif_occ/occ_mr_4326.rda"
source("../gbif_occ_maps/plot_occ_mr.R")
plot_facet + ggplot2::ggtitle("")

```

Finally, @fig-gbif-occ shows occurrences of Chinese muntjac in and around Flanders based on 
recent data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) [@gbif_the_global_biodiversity_information_facility_what_2025].
Occurrences are mapped on an OpenStreetMap tile projected in Web Mercator projection (ref OSM; ref ggspatial).
We include all observations within a bounding box around Flanders, holding a minimum distance of 30 km to the Flemish borders.
Each point represents a (validated or approved) occurrence. 
Points are displayed with a certain transparency level, such that overlaying (i.e., spatially clustered) observations 
appear more pronounced due to a more intense hue.
Occurrences belonging to data sets published by INBO are highlighted by colour (magenta).
These comprise the vast majority of the displayed observations (`r occ_mr$data_INBO |> sum()` out of `r occ_mr |> nrow()`),
and were collected in the context of the above mentioned camera trap-based monitoring in and around Park Vordenstein [@dhondt_muntjac_antwerp_2024] (ref section monitoring).


### Impact

An overview of the species' impacts is for instance given in @baiwy_risk_2013:

The species' impact on **vegetation and ecosystem functioning** is - in nature - comparable to that of other deer species:
it causes damage to forest understory, ground layer and shrub vegetation due to browsing and grazing.
The impact can be more severe for specific plant species, for instance ground level flowering plants. 
In terms of broader ecological consequences, the species can - especially if present at high densities - strongly modify the structure and composition of woodland vegetation, which in turn has cascading effects on animal communities depending on these ecosystems (e.g. reduced diversity of bird species nesting in understory vegetation) [see also @dhondt_monitoring_2023].

For **native deer species**, Chinese muntjac act as competitors for food and habitat, as well as disease vectors.

The **economic and social impact** includes limited impact on agricultural plantings, potentially severe damage to gardens and (unprotected) tree plantations. 
In addition, the species is often involved in road traffic accidents, which can cause human injuries or deaths.
